title: Practise 14 operations structuring questions, then compare your answers with model structures
description: 14 operations case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Reading about structuring only gets you so far. The skill comes from doing it, many times, with a clock running. Here are 14 real operations prompts. For each one, give yourself two minutes to sketch a structure on paper, say where you would start, then open the model answer and compare. Do not worry about matching it exactly; look for what you missed.
body:
1. A hospital's emergency waiting times have doubled in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Number of arrivals, by hour and day; Case mix: older, sicker patients take longer
  • Capacity: Doctors and nurses on shift vs arrivals; Cubicles and beds in the department
  • Process inside the department: Triage, tests, waiting for a specialist; Handovers between shifts
  • Flow out: Waiting for a ward bed upstairs; Discharges and social care delays

Where to start: Flow out: in most hospitals, patients waiting for a ward bed block the emergency department.

The trap: Only asking for more staff without checking whether patients are stuck waiting for beds.

2. A parcel company's on-time delivery fell from 95% to 85%.

Show a model structure
  • Where in the chain: Collection, sorting hub, linehaul, last mile; Which step has the delays?
  • Volume vs capacity: Parcel volume growth vs vans, drivers, sorting hours; Peaks by day and season
  • Process and systems: Route planning, scanning, missed handovers; New system or new hub recently?
  • External: Weather, traffic, partner carriers; Customer address and access problems

Where to start: Where in the chain: find the step where parcels start running late.

The trap: Listing causes without locating where in the chain delays start.

3. An airline's aircraft spend 20% longer on the ground between flights than rivals'.

Show a model structure
  • Arrival: Waiting for a gate, stand or tug; Taxi times
  • Aircraft servicing: Cleaning, catering, fuel, bags; Which task is on the critical path?
  • Boarding: Boarding process, cabin bags; Late passengers
  • Planning: Schedule buffers, crew connections; Staff numbers at peak

Where to start: The critical path: the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another sets the turnaround, so speeding up steps off that chain does nothing.

The trap: Trying to speed up every task when only the ones on the critical path matter.

4. A telecom company's customer complaints have tripled in six months.

Show a model structure
  • What they complain about: Billing, network, installation, support; Which category grew
  • Who complains: New vs existing customers; Region, product, channel they joined through
  • What changed: New billing system, price rise, outsourcing; Timing vs the rise
  • How we handle them: First-call resolution; Time to fix, repeat complaints

Where to start: What changed six months ago: a tripling rarely happens without a trigger.

The trap: Hiring more call-centre staff before finding the cause.

5. A furniture factory's defect rate rose from 2% to 6%.

Show a model structure
  • Where defects appear: Which product, line and process step; Which shift
  • Materials: Supplier changes, wood quality; Storage and humidity
  • People: New or temporary staff, training; Overtime and fatigue
  • Machines and process: Maintenance, settings, wear; New equipment or faster line speed

Where to start: Where defects appear: narrowing to one step usually reveals the cause.

The trap: Adding more inspection at the end instead of fixing the cause.

6. An airport's security queues now regularly exceed 45 minutes.

Show a model structure
  • Passenger demand: Passengers per hour by time of day; Flight schedule peaks
  • Lanes open: Staff rostered vs needed; Absence and hiring
  • Speed per lane: Bags rescanned, liquids, scanners; Passenger preparation
  • Layout and information: Space to queue and divest; Telling passengers when to arrive

Where to start: Demand by hour vs lanes open by hour: the mismatch is usually at peaks.

The trap: Asking for more scanners when the problem is staffing at the peak.

7. A pharmacy chain's shelves are out of stock on 8% of items.

Show a model structure
  • Which items: Fast movers vs long tail; Medicines vs retail products
  • Supply: Supplier shortages and late deliveries; Wholesaler fill rate
  • Ordering: Store forecasts and reorder points; System data errors
  • In-store: Stock in the back but not on the shelf; Shelf space and replenishment

Where to start: Which items: national medicine shortages and store ordering need different fixes.

The trap: Blaming suppliers without checking stock sitting in the stockroom.

8. A bank's app rating has fallen from 4.6 to 3.2 stars.

Show a model structure
  • What reviews say: Login, speed, crashes, missing features; When the bad reviews began
  • Which users: iPhone vs Android, device age; New vs existing customers
  • What changed: App release, new login security; Removed features
  • How we respond: Fix speed, release testing; Replying to reviews

Where to start: When the bad reviews began: line it up against releases.

The trap: Assuming it's a design problem without reading what users complain about.

9. Should an insurer outsource its IT support?

Show a model structure
  • Cost: Current cost vs vendor price; Transition and contract costs
  • Quality: Service levels, response times; Knowledge of our systems
  • Risk: Data security, regulation; Dependence on one vendor
  • Alternatives: Automate first, then outsource; Outsource only part

Where to start: Total cost including transition, against service levels.

The trap: Comparing salaries with the vendor's price and forgetting transition and oversight costs.

10. Should a US clothing brand move production from Asia to Mexico?

Show a model structure
  • Landed cost per item: Labour, fabric, freight, duties; Exchange rates
  • Speed and flexibility: Weeks from order to store; Less unsold stock and markdowns
  • Capability: Suppliers' skills and capacity; Quality
  • Risks and transition: Switching cost and time; Supply risk in each region

Where to start: Landed cost plus markdowns saved: speed is worth money in fashion.

The trap: Comparing factory prices only.

11. How can a traditional bank get more customers to use its app instead of branches?

Show a model structure
  • Reasons they don't: Trust, habit, missing features; Age and confidence
  • Make it better: Features people need in branches; Speed and reliability
  • Help people switch: Staff teaching in branches; Rewards for first use
  • Change defaults: Paperless statements; Fees for branch-only services

Where to start: Reasons they don't: missing features and low confidence need different fixes.

The trap: Pushing everyone online with fees before the app is good enough.

12. How can a call-centre business reduce staff turnover from 60% a year?

Show a model structure
  • Who leaves and when: New starters, shifts, teams; Exit reasons
  • Pay and hours: Pay vs local jobs; Shift patterns, flexibility
  • The job: Call targets, stress; Tools and training
  • Managers and growth: Team leaders' skills; Promotion paths

Where to start: Who leaves and when: many leave in the first three months, so check new starters first.

The trap: Raising pay for everyone before knowing why people leave.

13. How can a train operator get punctuality from 80% to 90%?

Show a model structure
  • Causes of delay: Track faults, train faults, staff, passengers; Which routes and times
  • Trains: Maintenance, spare trains; Faults per million miles
  • Timetable: Recovery time, platform use; Knock-on delays
  • People: Crew availability; Station dispatch

Where to start: Causes of delay: fix the few that cause most lost minutes.

The trap: Adding time to the timetable without fixing the causes.

14. How can a parcel company handle 50% more parcels at Christmas?

Show a model structure
  • Sorting capacity: Extra shifts, temporary sites; Automation
  • Delivery capacity: Temporary drivers and vans; Weekend and evening rounds
  • Shape demand: Customer cut-off dates, pricing; Lockers and pick-up points
  • Planning: Forecasts by customer; Hiring and training early

Where to start: Shape demand: spreading volume is cheaper than adding capacity.

The trap: Only hiring more people.
outro: Come back to these in a week and try them again. You will be surprised how much quicker the structures come. Want more? The free structuring drill has a timer and over 100 prompts.
